meta.blurb: Dev drives a taxi, and his back has stopped bending. Follow him through twelve weeks of ten-minute stretching with a retired teacher, and learn what flexibility is, what the evidence says, and how to start gently.
meta.bible: Dev: a taxi driver of about forty-eight, with a stiff back and a kind, dry sense of humour. Mrs Okafor: a retired school teacher of physical education who leads the free Tuesday class called Stretch for Ten Minutes in the community hall. Mr Lindqvist: a cheerful man of eighty-one in the class who stretches from a chair. Sam: a taxi driver and friend of Dev. The story runs for twelve weeks, from January to April. Key terms: Flexibility, Range of motion, Joint, Muscle, Tendon, Ligament, Calf, Hamstring, Quadriceps, Hip, Hips, Lunge, Spine, Shoulders, Chest, Neck, Wrist, Wrists, Ankles, Stretch, Stretching, Static, Dynamic, Warm up, Hypermobility, Physiotherapist, Yoga, Tai chi, Pilates, Reflex, Nervous system. The evidence is hedged where it is mixed: regular stretching reliably improves how far a joint can move; that stretching prevents injury or soreness is not clearly proven. A common suggestion is to hold each stretch for about thirty seconds; a stretch should feel like a pull and never like sharp pain. This book is general information and is not medical advice. Voice and tone: warm, practical, gently funny, honest about what is uncertain; no invented numbers, studies or quotes; no diagnosis and no personal treatment advice.

beats.summary: Static stretches are held still; dynamic stretches move through a range, like leg swings and arm circles.

B1B2: Dev has driven a taxi for twenty years, and these days his back feels stiff every morning. Yesterday he could hardly bend down far enough to tie his shoes.
At the library Dev sees a poster for a free class called Stretch for Ten Minutes. It meets on Tuesday mornings in the community hall, and he decides to try it.
Mrs Okafor, a retired teacher of physical education, welcomes the little group with a smile. Flexibility, she says, simply means how far your joints can move.
Muscles pull on the bones, and that is how we move. Tendons join the muscles to the bones, and ligaments hold the bones together at a joint.
Muscles tend to get used to the positions we keep them in. After years of sitting at the wheel, Dev's body has simply learned to stay still.
Scientists think that part of the gain from stretching happens in the nervous system. With practice, the brain seems to accept a deeper stretch as safe, so the body lets you go a little further.
Mrs Okafor teaches the first rule of the class. A stretch should feel like a firm pull, never like sharp pain, and if it hurts you ease off at once.
Before they stretch, everyone walks on the spot and swings their arms for two minutes. Warm muscles feel easier to stretch, so a short warm up is usually advised.
Slow breathing helps you to relax more deeply into a stretch. Mrs Okafor tells the group to breathe out as they move deeper and never to hold their breath.
Dev starts to bounce at the bottom of a stretch, but Mrs Okafor shakes her head. A sudden pull can make a muscle tighten up, so slow, steady holds are usually better.
The first stretch is for the calf, the muscle at the back of the lower leg. Dev leans on a wall with one leg behind him and holds the position for about thirty seconds.
Next comes the hamstring stretch, for the muscles along the back of the thigh. Dev sits on the edge of a chair, straightens one leg, and leans forward from his hips.
Dev cannot come close to touching his toes, and he laughs at himself. Mrs Okafor tells him that touching toes is not the goal, because the real aim is to move more comfortably in daily life.
Mrs Okafor shows Dev a trick for tight legs. Lying on his back, he loops a towel around one foot and lifts the leg up, so he never has to reach.
Some people bend easily and others do not, and that is perfectly normal. Bone shape, genes, age and daily habits all play a part, so Mrs Okafor says to compare yourself only with yourself.
The next stretch is for the quadriceps, the big muscle at the front of the thigh. Dev holds the back of a chair and gently pulls one foot toward his bottom.
Mrs Okafor shows a gentle kneeling lunge to open the front of the hip. Dev puts a cushion under his knee, steps one foot forward and shifts his weight slowly ahead.
At home Dev clears a space in his kitchen and does the whole routine again. It takes just ten minutes, and he finishes before the kettle has cooled.
Mrs Okafor suggests linking the new habit to something you already do. Dev decides to stretch every morning while the kettle boils, because he never forgets his tea.
In the second week the class turns to the shoulders and chest. Many people round forward over a wheel or a desk, so Dev clasps his hands behind his back and lifts them slowly.
The neck stretch is the gentlest and slowest of all the stretches. Dev lets his head tilt slowly toward one shoulder, and Mrs Okafor warns him never to force it with his hand.
On hands and knees, Dev slowly arches his back like an angry cat, then lets it sink down again. Mrs Okafor calls it the cat and cow, and it gently moves the whole spine.
Lying on his back, Dev hugs one knee toward his chest and feels his lower back relax. Mrs Okafor adds that pain that does not go away, or numbness in the legs, is a reason to see a doctor.
Mrs Okafor writes two words on a whiteboard: static and dynamic. A static stretch is held still, while a dynamic one moves a joint through its range, like a leg swing.
Before sport, many coaches prefer dynamic movements to long holds. Some studies suggest that holding a stretch for a long time right before a sprint or a jump may lower power for a short while.
Dev asks whether stretching can stop people from getting injuries. Mrs Okafor answers honestly that the evidence is mixed, although warm ups with several kinds of movement seem to help.

Another person asks a question about sore legs after a long walk. Reviews of the research find that stretching afterwards makes little clear difference to soreness the next day, but many people still enjoy it.
Dev notices that slow stretching feels calming, and that his busy mind goes quiet. Some people report this too, although scientists have not studied it as much as they have studied movement itself.
Mrs Okafor explains that strength and flexibility help each other. Moving through a full range while holding some weight, like a slow squat to a chair, can build both.
Between fares Dev gets out of the taxi at the rank, rolls his shoulders and stretches his calves. Regular short breaks from sitting matter more than most people realise.
By the fourth week, Dev finds that tying his shoes is easier than it was in January. The change is small and slow, and it has taken several weeks of regular practice.
One cold, wet morning, Dev feels as stiff as he did in January. Mrs Okafor tells him that cold weather, tiredness and poor sleep can all make a body feel tight, and it is not a failure.
A man in the class pushes too hard and strains a muscle in his leg. Mrs Okafor reminds everyone that stretching more is not better, and a little rest is part of the plan.

Some people are naturally very bendy, with joints that move further than average. For them, extra stretching is not the answer, and Mrs Okafor suggests strength work and advice from a physiotherapist.
Mrs Okafor tells the class that some people should ask a doctor first. That includes anyone with a recent injury, an operation, a joint replacement, pregnancy or a long-term health problem.
Mr Lindqvist is eighty-one years old, and he has not missed a single class. Flexibility tends to fall with age, but he shows that a lot of it can be kept.
Mr Lindqvist does all his stretches from a chair, so he never has to get down on the floor. A gentle seated twist, with one hand on the opposite knee, is his favourite.
Lying on his back, Dev lets both knees fall slowly to one side while his shoulders stay on the floor. It stretches the spine and hips, and Mrs Okafor says to go only as far as feels comfortable.
The feet carry the whole body all day, but they rarely get any attention. Dev circles his ankles, spreads his toes and points and flexes his feet.
Dev holds a steering wheel all day, so Mrs Okafor shows him a gentle wrist stretch. Palm up, he draws his fingers back with the other hand, and any numbness or tingling should be checked by a doctor.
Mrs Okafor writes down a simple plan for the ten minutes. It begins with two minutes of walking, then six stretches held for about thirty seconds on each side, and a minute of slow breathing.
Dev chooses his six stretches and sticks the list on his fridge. They are the calf, the hamstring, the hip, the chest, the upper back and the neck.
Dev hangs a calendar on the wall and marks a tick after each session. Soon he has a long line of ticks, and he does not want to break the chain.
In the eighth week Dev catches a bad cold and misses every session. When he is well again, Mrs Okafor tells him to start gently and not to feel guilty.
Dev shows his friend Sam a calf stretch against the taxi, and Sam laughs at him. A minute later he tries it too, and admits that it feels surprisingly good.
Some evenings Dev does a few slow stretches before bed, and they help him to wind down. Scientists have not shown that stretching improves sleep, but it does no harm and he enjoys it.
Stretching has taught Dev to notice his own body. Now he spots when his shoulders creep up toward his ears, or when his jaw is tight in traffic, and he lets them drop.
Mrs Okafor reminds the class that stretching is not the only way to keep supple. Yoga, tai chi and Pilates also build range of movement, and the best choice is the one you enjoy enough to keep doing.
By week twelve Dev can reach down to his shins without any strain, and he is delighted. Mrs Okafor reminds him that this is better than before, and that comfortable movement was always the point.
In April, Dev ties his shoes in the doorway, easily, then goes out into the spring morning. This book gives general information about stretching, and it is not medical advice.
C1C2: Dev had spent twenty years behind the wheel of a taxi, and his body had quietly kept the accounts. One grey Monday morning he sat on the edge of his bed and found that tying his shoes had become a small negotiation. It was nothing serious, he told himself, but it was the kind of thing that makes a man wonder where the years have gone.

While waiting for a fare outside the library, Dev wandered in and noticed a hand-painted poster promising a free class called Stretch for Ten Minutes. It was held on Tuesday mornings in the community hall, and the organiser had added, in friendly capitals, that nobody needed to be fit or bendy. Dev read it twice, told himself he was only curious, and wrote down the time before he could change his mind.

Mrs Okafor, a retired teacher of physical education with a voice built for crowded playgrounds, welcomed the small group as though each person were an old friend. Flexibility, she told them, is nothing mysterious: it is the range of movement that a joint can comfortably travel through. Everyone has some, she added with a warm smile, and almost everyone can have a little more of it if they practise.

Using a faded chart pinned beside the piano, Mrs Okafor reminded the group that muscles move the body by pulling on bones. Tendons are the strong cords that fasten muscle to bone, she said, while ligaments hold one bone to another across every joint. Between them they decide how freely a knee, a shoulder or a hip will move.

Muscles, Mrs Okafor explained, adapt to the positions in which we keep them, and a body that sits for hours every day becomes very good at sitting. Dev recognised himself at once, because his working life had been a long, patient rehearsal of one posture. Stiffness, she assured him, was not a punishment but the natural result of habit.

Research suggests that some of the improvement from regular stretching has less to do with muscles growing longer than with the nervous system growing more tolerant. Gradually, the brain learns that a deeper stretch is not a threat, and it allows the muscle to relax further. Scientists are still debating how much of the change is of each kind, Mrs Okafor admitted, but the result for the person stretching is the same.

The first rule of the class, Mrs Okafor announced, was also the most important: a stretch should feel like a firm, steady pull and never like a sharp or burning pain. If a movement hurts, she said, the sensible response is to ease off at once, because the body is not a negotiator that rewards stubbornness. Dev, who had spent his life being proud of pushing on, found this oddly hard to accept.

Before a single stretch was attempted, the whole group marched on the spot, swinging their arms and breathing a little harder than usual. Warm muscles tend to feel looser and more willing to lengthen, Mrs Okafor said, and so a couple of minutes of gentle movement is the usual advice. It was undignified for the first thirty seconds and rather pleasant for the rest.

Breathing, according to Mrs Okafor, is the part of stretching that most people forget as soon as they start concentrating on the rest. She asked them to breathe slowly through the nose and to let the breath out as they moved a little deeper, because a held breath usually means a tensed body. It sounded too simple to matter, yet Dev felt his shoulders drop for the first time all week.

Halfway through the first stretch, Dev began to bounce at the bottom of the movement, in the manner of a man trying to start a stubborn engine. Mrs Okafor stopped him kindly and explained that a quick pull may cause a muscle to tighten in self-defence, which is exactly the opposite of what he wanted. A slow, steady hold, she said, gives the muscle enough time to let go, and the body is rarely in a hurry to argue.

The first stretch was for the calf, the thick muscle at the back of the lower leg that every driver uses and nobody thanks. Dev leaned his hands against the wall, stepped one foot back with the heel pressed down, and felt a slow pull gather behind his knee. Thirty seconds is a common suggestion for a hold, Mrs Okafor said, and then the other leg must have its turn.

The hamstrings run along the back of the thigh from the hip to just below the knee, and in people who sit a great deal they often feel like tightly tuned guitar strings. Dev perched on the front edge of a chair, straightened one leg with the heel resting on the floor, and tipped forward from his hips with a long back. The pull was immediate, honest and not at all dramatic, and it settled into something pleasantly warm after twenty seconds or so.

Dev stretched his fingers toward his toes, found them considerably farther away than he remembered, and laughed at the distance. Mrs Okafor assured him that reaching the toes is a party trick rather than a target, and that the proper aim of the class was to move more comfortably through an ordinary day. Nobody, she added, had ever been asked at a job interview whether they could touch their toes.

For anyone whose arms refuse to meet their legs halfway, Mrs Okafor produced a simple remedy from her bag: an old towel. Dev lay on his back, looped it around the sole of one foot and drew the straightened leg gently upward, feeling the familiar pull along the back of the thigh without any of the struggle. Props, she said, are not cheating, but a clever way of bringing the floor closer.

Within a few minutes the group looked like a gallery of different bodies, some folding easily and others stopping early with an air of dignified resignation. Bone shape, inherited traits, age and long habit all influence how far a joint will go, Mrs Okafor said, and no one controls all of them. The only fair comparison, she concluded, is between you today and you in a month's time.

For the front of the thigh, where the large quadriceps muscle sits, Mrs Okafor offered a chair as a steadying friend. Dev held its back with one hand, bent a knee, caught his ankle and drew his heel gently toward his seat, wobbling a little before he found his balance. The knees should stay close together, she reminded him, and the back should not arch.

The kneeling lunge, she explained, opens the front of the hip, which spends the whole working day folded in half beneath a steering wheel. With a cushion under his back knee, Dev stepped his other foot forward and let his weight drift slowly ahead, until a pleasant stretch appeared deep in the hip. It felt like unfolding a letter that had been creased for years and left at the bottom of a drawer.

That evening Dev cleared a patch of kitchen floor, set a timer on his phone and worked through everything he could remember from the class. Ten minutes sounded laughably small, yet by the end he was warm, slightly out of breath and strangely satisfied. He suspected that the secret was in its modesty, since no one could claim to be too busy for ten minutes.

Mrs Okafor had a theory that new habits survive best when they are fastened to old ones, and she advised the group to choose something they already did without thinking. Dev chose the kettle, a ritual he had never once forgotten in twenty years, and promised himself to stretch while it boiled. Within a week the rising roar of the water heating had become his cue, as dependable as a bell in a school corridor.

By the second Tuesday the group had moved up the body to the shoulders and chest, which tend to curl forward in anyone who drives, types or scrolls for a living. Dev clasped his hands behind his back, straightened his arms and lifted them a little, feeling the front of his chest open like a pair of shutters. Mrs Okafor reminded him to keep his ribs drawn down, his neck relaxed and his breathing slow while he held the position.

Necks, Mrs Okafor said, deserve the most patient treatment of any part of the body, because they are narrow, busy and not at all fond of being hurried. Dev let his head tip slowly toward one shoulder, with his other arm hanging loose, and simply waited for the stretch to come to him. Nothing should be pushed or pulled hard, she warned, and anyone with a neck problem should ask a professional before trying it.

On hands and knees, with his wrists below his shoulders, Dev arched his back toward the ceiling like a startled cat and then let it sink slowly the other way. Mrs Okafor called the movement the cat and cow, and she said it is a kind way to coax the spine through its range, one small segment at a time. He felt, absurdly, like a very large kitten, and he was surprised to find that the feeling was an agreeable one.

Lying flat on the mat, Dev drew one knee toward his chest and felt the base of his spine let go with something close to a sigh. This is a gentle movement that many people enjoy, Mrs Okafor said, but she made it very clear that back pain which lingers, or numbness and weakness in the legs, should be examined by a doctor rather than stretched. Stretching, she reminded them gently, is a useful habit but it is not a cure for everything, and it should never replace proper medical advice.

On the whiteboard Mrs Okafor wrote two words, static and dynamic, and then explained them with the patience of a woman who had taught the difference to a thousand schoolchildren. A static stretch is held in one place, she said, whereas a dynamic one carries a joint smoothly through its range, as in a controlled leg swing or a wide circle of the arms. Both have their uses at different moments, she said, and neither of them is the winner in every situation.

Before sport, Mrs Okafor said, many coaches favour dynamic warm ups, such as leg swings and arm circles, over long static holds. Some studies have found that holding a stretch for a minute or more immediately before a sprint or a jump may reduce power for a short time, though the effect is small and not equally clear in every study. Dev, whose only sport was parking, noted this with polite interest and decided that it would not trouble him until the Olympics.

Dev asked the question that everyone had been waiting to ask: does stretching protect you from injury? Mrs Okafor replied with refreshing honesty that the research is mixed, and that stretching alone has not been clearly shown to prevent injuries, though a warm up combining several kinds of movement does seem to help in sport. She preferred, she said, to promise only what she could prove, and she would rather disappoint a hopeful student than mislead one.

Another member of the class asked whether stretching after a long walk would prevent aching legs the next morning. Careful reviews of the research, Mrs Okafor replied, have found little clear effect on that kind of soreness, which tends to pass in a day or two whatever one does. Many people stretch afterwards all the same, she added, simply because it feels pleasant and gives the body a calm way to finish.

Somewhere in the third week Dev noticed that the stretching was doing something other than lengthening his hamstrings. The slow breathing and the unhurried attention seemed to switch off the chatter in his head, and he left the hall feeling lighter than he had arrived. Many people describe the same effect, Mrs Okafor said, although the research on it is thinner than the research on movement itself.

Flexibility without strength is only half of the picture, Mrs Okafor said, because a joint needs muscles that can control it throughout its range. Moving slowly through a full range under a modest load, as in a deep squat to a chair, trains both qualities together. Dev, who had always assumed that strong people were stiff and bendy people weak, felt a long-held belief quietly dissolve.

Between fares at the station rank, Dev began to climb out of his taxi, roll his shoulders, circle his ankles and stretch his calves against the bumper. His colleagues, who had known him for years, watched with the guarded amusement of men who suspected a passing phase and were prepared to wait. Frequent short breaks from sitting matter, Mrs Okafor had told him, and a couple of minutes upright every hour or so is a sound habit for anyone who works while seated.

By the fourth week, Dev tied his shoes one morning without a single grunt, and he sat there for a moment, wondering whether anything had happened. Studies of regular stretching suggest that small gains in range of movement often show within a few weeks, though they arrive slowly and quietly rather than in dramatic leaps. It was not a miracle, but it was unmistakably better, and he found himself grinning at his own feet like a schoolboy.

One bitter, rainy morning Dev woke feeling every bit as stiff as he had in January, and his spirits sank accordingly. Mrs Okafor, unmoved, told him that cold, tiredness, a poor night's sleep and the time of day all influence how loose a body feels, and that progress is a trend rather than a straight line. A bad morning, she said kindly, is not a verdict on the whole programme, and tomorrow's body may be quite a different character.

One Tuesday a newcomer, eager to catch up, pushed so far into a hamstring stretch that he felt something pull and had to sit out the rest of the class. Mrs Okafor was sympathetic but firm: more is not better, and a muscle that is forced beyond comfort can be strained. Patience, she said, was the quickest route to progress, however inconvenient that sounded to a man in a hurry to catch up with the others.

A young woman at the back of the class could bend her thumb to touch her wrist and fold herself in half without apparent effort. Mrs Okafor explained that some people have unusually mobile joints, sometimes called hypermobility, and that such people generally need strength and control more than additional stretching. If a joint ever feels unstable or painful, she said, a physiotherapist is the right person to ask.

Before the lesson began that day, Mrs Okafor reminded the class that general advice cannot fit every body. Anyone with a recent injury or operation, a joint replacement, thinning bones, a pregnancy or a long-term health condition, she said, should ask a doctor or physiotherapist what is suitable before starting any new routine. It was said briskly, without alarm, in the tone of someone who had said it a hundred times.

Mr Lindqvist, a white-haired gentleman of eighty-one, had not missed a Tuesday in three years, and he stretched with a quiet, concentrated pleasure that Dev found rather moving. Flexibility generally declines as we grow older, Mrs Okafor said, but the decline is not as steep or as certain as people fear, and regular movement helps to keep much of what we have. Mr Lindqvist, she added with evident affection, was the best advertisement for the class that she owned, and he worked for nothing.

Mr Lindqvist preferred never to meet the floor, and so his entire routine took place on a sturdy chair. His favourite was a gentle seated twist, in which he turned his shoulders slowly to one side with a hand on the opposite knee and looked over his shoulder like a man hearing a distant bell. Anyone could borrow his method, Mrs Okafor said, and many of the class did.

Lying on his back with his arms stretched wide, Dev let both bent knees fall slowly to one side and felt a long, gentle twist travel up his spine. The shoulders should stay on the floor, Mrs Okafor reminded him, and the knees need go no farther than feels comfortable, since the point is ease rather than acrobatics. He turned his head the opposite way and let the floor do most of the work.

Feet, Mrs Okafor observed, carry the entire weight of the body all day and receive almost no gratitude in return. Dev sat on his mat, drew slow circles with each ankle, spread his toes as wide as they would go, and pointed and flexed his feet in turn. His toes, long confined to driving shoes, seemed astonished to be consulted, and a little ashamed of how long they had been ignored.

Hands that grip a steering wheel for hours deserve some care, Mrs Okafor told him, and she showed him a stretch for the wrists and forearms. With his arm straight and his palm facing away, Dev drew his fingers gently back with the other hand until he felt a mild pull, and then let go slowly. Numbness or tingling in the hands, she added, is something to mention to a doctor rather than to stretch away.

At the end of the class Mrs Okafor wrote out a plan that she said would fit inside any life. Two minutes of gentle walking on the spot would come first, followed by six stretches, each held for about thirty seconds on each side. A final minute of slow breathing would close the session, and the rest of the ten would be spent moving between stretches, which was so modest a demand, Dev thought, that it was almost impossible to argue with.

That evening Dev made his own list of six stretches, choosing those that complained loudest, and stuck it to his fridge with a magnet shaped like a taxi. They were the calf, the hamstring, the front of the hip, the chest, the upper back and the neck, in an order that moved naturally from the floor to the ceiling. The routine, he found, took him exactly as long as an episode of the radio news.

Dev hung a cheap calendar on the kitchen wall and drew a tick on each day he stretched, a trivial ceremony that soon proved oddly powerful. By the end of the month the ticks formed a long, satisfying chain, and he found that he did not wish to be the man who broke it. Mrs Okafor approved, though she insisted that a missed day should be a pause and never a disaster.

In the eighth week Dev caught a heavy cold and missed an entire week, ticks and all, and he returned to the hall feeling as if he had lost everything. Mrs Okafor greeted him without any reproach and told him to begin again gently, at perhaps two thirds of his former effort. The body, she said, forgets a little during a break, but it relearns far faster than it learned the first time.

At the rank, Dev demonstrated the calf stretch against the side of his cab to his old friend Sam, who laughed so hard he had to lean on the roof. Within a minute, however, Sam had stopped mocking and begun copying, and he was soon admitting, with a grimace that became a smile, that it felt rather good. Habits, Dev reflected, spread far more easily by example than by lecture, and he resolved to lecture rather less and stretch rather more.

On some evenings Dev took to doing two or three very slow stretches beside the bed, with the lamp turned low and the radio off. Whether stretching truly improves sleep has not been firmly proven, Mrs Okafor cautioned, but many people find that unhurried movement helps them to put the day down. Dev slept well, whatever the explanation, and did not feel the need to argue with his luck.

Perhaps the most unexpected result of the weeks of stretching was that Dev had begun to notice his own body in a way he never had before. In the middle of a traffic jam he would catch his shoulders hovering near his ears or his jaw clamped like a vice, and he would let them fall with a long breath. Awareness, Mrs Okafor said, is the quiet teacher inside every good stretch, and it is a lesson that follows you out of the hall.

Stretching on a mat is only one road to a supple body, Mrs Okafor reminded them, and she pinned photographs of yoga, tai chi and Pilates classes to the noticeboard. All of them train the range of movement, along with balance and control, and none is inherently better than another. The best exercise, she said, is whichever one you enjoy enough to repeat for years.

At the end of the twelfth week, Dev bent forward from his hips and found that his fingertips travelled comfortably as far as his shins, a journey that had once seemed impossible. His toes remained a rumour, but Mrs Okafor reminded him that the point was never a spectacular result, only ease in the ordinary actions of a life. He agreed, and was quietly pleased to find that he truly meant it, which was not something he could have said in January.

On a bright morning in April, Dev bent over in his doorway, tied his shoes in a moment, and stepped out into the spring light with an ease that surprised him. Stretching is a small, kind habit, but this book gives general information only and is not medical advice, so anyone with an injury, a health condition or any doubt should ask a doctor first. For everyone else, ten gentle minutes tomorrow is a perfectly good place to begin.
